name: Aduge
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Spurious languoid: Glottolog retired it for bookkeeping — Aduge is an Okpamheri-speaking village, not a distinct language; no description exists.

new_statements.quote: [1989 p.95] Ibilo exhibits a 'two tone plus downstep' system. There is no evidence of synchronic downdrifting in my data, although Akinlabi (1979) rather routinely claimed downdrift exists in Ibilo. ... The downstep in Ibilo is limited in occurrence and is unlikely to be successfully analysed as a 'mid' tone. [1973 p.263] Two levels of pitch are significant in Ibilo: high and low. The two levels contrast minimally ... Note that the high is of the level commonly called 'mid' ... There is a third level of tone in Ibilo which is not identified in lexical items. The third level is of limited occurrence and is seen here (as in Egene, Urhobo, etc.) as (non-automatic) downstep.

There is no evidence of synchronic downdrifting in my data, although Akinlabi (1979) rather routinely claimed downdrift exists in Ibilo. One notices that Akinlabi presents no instrumental evidence of down drift.. The downstep in Ibilo is limited in occurrence and is unlikely to be successfully analysed as a 'mid' tone." The reader's quote is verbatim; the only differences are text-layer scanned glitches ('imid'' for 'mid') and the marked ellipsis. Surrounding section read (4.17.1 syllable…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Okpamheri (described through its Ibilo dialect) is a register tone language with two lexical tones (H, L) plus a non-automatic downstep; neither Elugbe 1973 nor Elugbe 1989 says anything about word stress or accent, and the only source with Aduge data (Decker et al. 2024) analysed neither tone nor stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; Elugbe 1973 p.265 notes LL disyllabic nouns surface as high-falling-low, and Elugbe 1989 p.42 notes shortened/devoiced final vowels in some Ibilo disyllabic stems (not framed as stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on nouns/verbs in citation form and short phrases; statement is for the Ibilo dialect of Okpamheri, not for Aduge/Uma speech itself.
new_statements.identity_note: adug1238 is a Glottolog bookkeeping (spurious) languoid: Ethnologue's Aduge [adu] is 'an Okpamheri [opa]-speaking village' (Jungraithmayr & Ganslmayr 1986:39), i.e. part of Okpamheri okpa1238. Decker et al. 2024 (SIL survey, fieldwork in Aduge 2022) confirm: the Evaduge are ethnically Yoruba and 'adopted their current language from the village of Imoga. The people in Imoga speak Uma, a dialect of Okpamheri'; mutual intelligibility with Imoga reported. The tone statement quoted is for the Ibilo dialect of Okpamheri (formerly ibil1238/[ibi], merged into [opa] in 2012), not for Aduge/Uma speech; Elugbe 1989 describes another Okpamheri variety, Emhalhe (Somorika), as having three tone levels, so prosodic detail varies within the cluster. Any catalog entry belongs under okpa1238, not adug1238.

sources.note: Okpamheri treated via its Ibilo dialect (sec. 4.17, pp. 94-96) and Emhalhe/Somorika (sec. 4.16). sec. 4.17.8 Tone p.95: "Ibilo exhibits a 'two tone plus downstep' system." sec. 4.16.8: Emhalhe has three distinctive levels. p.42: final-vowel shortening in Ibilo disyllabic stems. sources.note: Only modern first-hand source with Aduge data (fieldwork Aduge 7 Sept 2022; 222-item Aduge wordlist, Appendix F; sec. 8.3 pooled phonetic inventories incl. 'the Uma dialect of Okpamheri as spoken in Imoga and Aduge'). Appendix F p.48: 'The transcriptions are preliminary since there was no analysis of tones and no in-depth analysis of other phonological or phonetic features.' Nothing on stress or accent; tone not analysed. Sec. 4 p.6 names Abiodun (1983) 'Aduge phonology' and Ogunwale (1985) 'Aduge verbs' (Ilorin B.A. papers).
